Scattering of quasiparticles provides direct access to the interactions that govern strongly correlated systems. In this work, we realize the quasiparticle scattering experiment of the Fermi-Hubbard model on a digital quantum processor by colliding a doublon and a holon in the half-filled chain of 21 sites encoded on 42 qubits of the ibm_boston processor. For the first time, we measure the transmission probability of quasiparticles of the Hubbard model on quantum hardware, which agrees with the Bethe-ansatz scattering matrix without free parameters. Beyond the scattering probabilities, the collision generates entanglement by superposing the transmitted and reflected components, which we infer from the particle-number fluctuation. In sharp contrast, a control collision between two doublons shows neither the interaction dependence nor the number fluctuation, as expected for indistinguishable particles. Our work demonstrates that the ability to create quasiparticles of a chosen flavor on demand and program their motion and interactions makes a digital quantum processor a new experimental toolset for probing the entanglement structure generated by quasiparticle scattering.

These results provide a quantitative representation of magnetic-orientation-dependent Berry-curvature dipoles and show how carrier occupation influences both the response and its predictability.

Recent progress in programmable quantum simulators motivates exact benchmarks for nonequilibrium dynamics in topological quantum matter. We study the Kitaev honeycomb model driven through its critical regions by a linear ramp of the bond coupling $J_z$ over a ramp time $τ$, comparing zigzag and armchair ribbons with fully periodic tubes. The production of excitations exhibits a geometry-dependent finite-size crossover controlled by $N_2/\sqrtτ$, the ratio of the ribbon width to the Kibble--Zurek length. Periodic tubes obey the expected critical-line Kibble--Zurek scaling and serve as the boundary-free benchmark. Zigzag ribbons follow the same scaling until defect production is exponentially suppressed by a finite-width algebraic gap floor associated with the formation of Majorana edge modes, whose occupation is pinned by inversion parity. Armchair ribbons instead support transient Majorana edge modes with exponentially small gaps, producing width-parity-dependent defect plateaus: exactly one defect per unit length for odd widths and an approximate, transient plateau near one half for even widths. The quench-generated entanglement entropy and fermionic logarithmic negativity inherit the same geometry-dependent structure, and the negativity further distinguishes the coherence-borne entanglement of the Kibble--Zurek regime from the population-borne entanglement of the edge-mode plateaus. These results identify boundary Majorana modes as the mechanism controlling departures from ideal Kibble--Zurek dynamics and provide geometry-resolved benchmarks for programmable simulations of topological matter.

We present ToF-PAX-RIXS, a compact instrument that combines time-of-flight momentum-microscopy angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) with resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS). The latter is based on photoelectron spectrometry for analysis of X-rays (PAX). The two techniques are implemented with a single multimode electron-optical column, allowing measurements to be performed sequentially on the same sample under identical experimental conditions. In ARPES mode, the instrument records the photoemission intensity as a function of kinetic energy and two in-plane momentum components. In PAX-RIXS mode, scattered soft X-ray photons are absorbed in a thin metallic converter, and the generated photoelectrons are analyzed in energy and position of emission on the converter. The electron kinetic energy retains the spectral information of the scattered photons, while the position is related to the scattering angle and therefore to the momentum transfer, enabling simultaneous access to a finite momentum-transfer interval. We describe the mechanical design, converter assembly, scattering geometry, and multimode electron optics of the instrument. Its PAX-RIXS performance is benchmarked at the Cu $L_3$ edge using CaCuO$_2$, with Au, Ag, and Pt converters. The measured spectra reproduce the principal features obtained with a conventional grating RIXS spectrometer, and deconvolution yields an effective reconstructed energy resolution better than $120$~meV under the present conditions. Finally, combined ARPES and PAX-RIXS measurements on the same Ca-doped YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.45}$ sample demonstrate the capability of the instrument to correlate electronic structure and collective excitations within a common compact platform.

Magic in quantum trajectory unravelings of noisy random quantum circuits

Sara Santos Alessio Paviglianiti Vincenzo Savona
arXiv:2610.22318v1 Published: 2026-10-15 LLM Score: 0.800 dmrg_preprints

The quantum-trajectory description of a noisy quantum circuit is not unique: every Kraus representation of the noise channel defines a different unraveling, i.e., a different ensemble of pure states that averages to the same density matrix. While all unravelings share the same expectation values of observables, they generally differ in the amount of quantum resources carried by the individual trajectories. Here we study non-stabilizerness, or magic, quantified by the stabilizer Rényi entropy, in quantum-trajectory unravelings of Haar-random and $T$-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits subject to local dephasing noise of strength $p$. The canonical unraveling in terms of Pauli jumps is Clifford and leaves magic untouched, so that trajectories retain the Haar-random value of non-stabilizerness. Exploring the full two-parameter family of minimal unravelings, we find that the trajectory-averaged magic can be substantially reduced by a state-independent choice of Kraus operators, and that the optimal choice is not in general the projective-measurement unraveling, but a two-outcome generalized measurement in which the Kraus operators correspond to a weak measurement of the noisy qubit. The optimal unraveling reduces the extensive magic density of the trajectories by a $p$-dependent factor without altering its linear scaling with system size. At the same time, it produces a very broad distribution of magic over trajectories, with a sizable fraction of trajectories retaining Haar-random magic. Since the cost of stabilizer-based classical simulation grows exponentially with the magic of the state, these high-magic trajectories, rather than the average, control the simulation cost. Our results delineate the potential and the limitations of unraveling optimization as a route to the classical simulation of noisy quantum dynamics with stabilizer methods.

Can quantum communication determine the size of an anonymous network when no size bound is known? Classical impossibility proofs rely on the covering lemma: an execution can be reproduced on a larger network with the same local structure. Quantum interference invalidates this argument - a measurement record possible on a network can become impossible on a cover. We show that the impossibility of exact counting nevertheless survives. Our main result is a quantum analogue of the covering lemma that preserves local possibilities rather than complete executions. Within a cyclic covering family, every local measurement outcome possible at a node remains possible at a corresponding node in every sufficiently large network. This holds even after information has travelled around the smaller network, beyond the reach of a simple locality argument. We extend the principle to the universal covering tree and finite covers with sufficiently long cycles. The proof combines tensor-network methods with graph coverings: a common representation across network sizes turns normalization into a constraint on which local outcomes can occur. For uniform synchronous protocols with independently prepared nodes, this support-lifting principle rules out zero-error counting and even the production of a guaranteed finite size bound on anonymous rings and the other cyclic covering families considered here. It also rules out exact leader election with termination in finite time with probability one on these families. Measurements, classical control, and local memory growing with time are allowed; no predetermined running-time bound is assumed. Quantum interference thus defeats execution lifting without enabling infallible certification of network size.

We investigate magnetic correlations in the two-leg Kondo-Hubbard ladder using the density-matrix renormalization group method. We focus on a parameter regime in which the noninteracting electronic system has a narrow indirect band gap. In this regime, there is no Fermi surface, and the conventional Fermi-surface-based Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida picture is not directly applicable; magnetic correlations between localized spins become weaker as the noninteracting band gap increases. We find that a moderate on-site Coulomb interaction enhances the antiferromagnetic correlations between localized spins. This enhancement, which is also seen in the staggered magnetization induced by a pinning field at the edges, occurs for both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Kondo couplings. Our results show that electron-electron interactions can enhance magnetic correlations between localized spins even when the underlying noninteracting electronic structure is gapped, suggesting an interaction-driven route to magnetic instabilities in narrow-gap Kondo-lattice systems.

Recent experiments in monolayer and trilayer graphene have observed incompressible even-denominator fractional quantum Hall states within narrow regions of parameter space associated with crossings of zeroth Landau levels. This is surprising because at half filling the Coulomb interaction in the zeroth Landau level is expected to favour a compressible composite Fermi liquid. Here we provide the first quantitative energetic study of the candidate incompressible phases and of the microscopic mechanisms that can stabilise them near such Landau-level crossings. Using exact diagonalization and infinite density-matrix renormalisation group, we first study ultra-short-range corrections to the Coulomb interaction arising from finite layer separation, lattice-scale effects, and electron-phonon coupling. We find that a sufficiently strong attractive short-range interaction drives the composite Fermi liquid first into a weakly paired \(d\)-wave pseudospin-singlet state and subsequently into a strongly paired state. However, microscopic estimates of these short-range corrections are far too small to stabilise either incompressible phase. We then incorporate Landau-level mixing through screening within the random-phase approximation. Screening substantially reshapes the effective interaction, suppresses the weak-pairing regime, and strongly enhances the tendency toward strong pairing. For a realistic range of microscopic parameters, the strongly paired phase is stabilised over a substantial fraction of that range. Frustrated magnets host rich emergent behavior because competing interactions generate dense manifolds of low-energy states. The Ising Shastry-Sutherland model is a paradigmatic setting, motivated experimentally by Ising-like rare-earth tetraborides such as TmB$_4$ and ErB$_4$, whose field-induced magnetization plateaus have motivated extensive microscopic modeling. Yet how tunable quantum fluctuations reorganize this material-motivated phase diagram remains largely unexplored. Here, we realize a transverse- and longitudinal-field Ising model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice using a programmable Rydberg-atom array. We map its quantum phase diagram using density matrix renormalization group calculations and probe corresponding signatures experimentally in arrays containing more than 110 atoms. Beyond the established classical phases, the calculations identify two regimes absent in the classical limit and stabilized at finite transverse field: a $2/5$ filling plateau whose finite stability region emerges from a classically degenerate phase boundary and a symmetry-preserving quantum-dimer regime replacing classically selected collinear order. Experiments on finite open arrays reveal signatures consistent with these regimes across three boundary-pinning conditions, with the resulting response maps agreeing qualitatively with the calculated phase diagram. Our results establish programmable Rydberg-atom arrays as tools for exploring frustrated, material-motivated Hamiltonians and motivate searches for new, quantum-driven magnetization plateaus and quantum-dimer behavior in ErB$_4$ under a transverse field or in strain-tuned TmB$_4$.

We show how to perform exact diagonalization of SU($N$)-symmetric Bose-Hubbard models separately in each irreducible representation of SU($N$), by exploiting the Howe duality between U($L$) and U($N$). Three structural consequences follow for any lattice and any Hamiltonian built from the U($L$) generators: (i) the spectrum in a given orbital sector is independent of $N$ and of the particle statistics, (ii) the canonical partition functions for bosons and fermions obey the exact identity $Z_{\mathrm{b}}(-N)=(-1)^{N_\mathrm{b}}Z_{\mathrm{f}}(N)$, (iii) with unfrustrated hopping the groundstate is always a color ferromagnet, so that the color-resolved method we introduce is useful to study excited sectors, frustrated lattices and finite temperatures. As applications, we first derive the finite-temperature phase diagram of attractive SU($N$) bosons on few-site rings at large $N$ for arbitrary filling. We then show the emergence of singlet-cluster states from frustrated hopping, the counterpart of fermionic ferromagnetism, with the example of the sawtooth and kagome lattice.

Fractional spin excitations in low-dimensional and frustrated magnets are commonly associated with sporadic spin fluctuations, as observed in quantum spin liquids, spin ices, and other complex magnetic states. In this study, we investigate the spin dynamics in the amplitude-modulated magnetic ground state of AgCuVO$_4$, a spin-1/2 chain compound with competing intrachain interactions, by muon spectroscopy. Our data reveal a Gaussian decay of muon polarization that remains remarkably resilient against applied magnetic fields---a behavior often interpreted as evidence of emergent sporadic spin dynamics. However, density functional theory calculations of muon stopping sites and their quadrupolar level-crossing resonance spectra suggest an alternative mechanism: a two-state model where the muon randomly hops between two nearby sites, eventually equilibrating across both on a microsecond timescale via quantum delocalization. These findings provide a microscopic explanation for the field-resilient muon polarization and indicate that such behavior may not always stem from intrinsic spin fluctuations, but can also arise from non-equilibrium muon dynamics.

We demonstrate the emergence of extraordinary-log criticality in a quantum many-body system by coupling a spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg chain to a two-dimensional quantum critical Heisenberg bilayer. Under the quantum-to-classical mapping, the chain acts as a plane defect in a three-dimensional critical environment for which the extraordinary-log universality class has recently been predicted. Using large-scale sign-problem-free quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we directly probe the renormalization-group flow of the effective defect coupling through the spin stiffness. We observe the characteristic logarithmic growth with linear system size $L$, corresponding to a stable weak-coupling fixed point and a running coupling $g(L)\sim 1/\log L$. Furthermore, the extracted step-scaling function quantitatively follows the universal renormalization-group flow predicted for the extraordinary-log universality class, including the leading and subleading universal coefficients. Our results establish extraordinary-log criticality in a genuine quantum many-body setting and show that its universal behavior persists despite the topological $θ$-term present in the low-energy field theory of the isolated spin chain.

Quantum skyrmions in frustrated spin-$1/2$ magnets are bound states of a few flipped spins in a ferromagnetic background. Using exact diagonalization and density-matrix renormalization group calculations for the $J_1$--$J_2$ triangular-lattice model with easy-axis anisotropy $K$, we ask what happens when two such objects are brought together. The binding energy per flipped spin of a single skyrmion has a minimum at $\Nf^{*}=7$ for $K=0.02$--$0.04$, and skyrmions smaller than $\Nf^{*}$ do not exist as pairs: at any distance they coalesce into a single larger object, and pinning wells cannot prevent it. Two skyrmions of natural size, by contrast, form a bound molecule without pinning or external field, with binding energy $U\simeq-0.007J_1$ at $K=0.03$--$0.04$ and an equilibrium separation of $5.5$ lattice spacings that does not depend on $K$ or on the size of the simulation domain; at $K=0.02$, where the single skyrmion is itself marginally bound, the pair is unbound within our resolution. The two constituents keep their identity ($7+7$ flipped spins) and are coupled by a coherent exchange of magnons, visible as number fluctuations between the two halves of the domain in excess of those of two independent skyrmions and as in-plane spin correlations between the two skyrmion walls that reach $0.16$ across the gap. These correlations follow the vortex pattern of the two textures and lock their relative helicity, the quantum counterpart of the helicity-dependent interaction of classical skyrmions. We discuss the molecule as a self-assembled two-qubit element for skyrmion helicity qubits in a single layer.

Two quantum skyrmions in a frustrated spin-$1/2$ magnet bind into a molecule, and the molecule acts as a magnon Josephson junction: the relative helicity $θ$ and the number $n$ of magnons transferred between them obey $H=E_Cn^2-W\cosθ$. DMRG on the $J_1$--$J_2$ triangular lattice gives $E_C$ as the curvature of the skyrmion energy at its natural size of seven flipped spins, and the measured helicity coherence fixes $W\simeq0.02J_1$, half the skyrmion--antiskyrmion tunnel splitting and independent of the anisotropy. Two helicity qubits side by side are thus strongly coupled by their own interaction.

Defect engineering is a crucial tool for tuning and tailoring the properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials. A key challenge is identifying which defects are kinetically stable at room temperature and sufficiently promising to warrant further investigation. However, identifying stable defects with suitable properties using first-principles calculations, such as density functional theory (DFT) is computationally demanding, effectively limiting the scope of high-throughput studies. In this work, we investigate whether the machine learning interatomic potential MACE can reproduce sorption trends (adsorption vs. absorption) previously obtained from high-throughput DFT calculations and extend the analysis to elevated temperatures. A total of 17,624 defect structures from the ADAQ database are simulated using MACE-accelerated molecular dynamics (MD) at both 0 K and 300 K. The results show that MACE successfully reproduces the overall sorption trends observed in DFT calculations at 0 K at a fraction of the computational cost. Simulations performed at 300 K further indicate that the qualitative sorption trends remain largely the same when including finite-temperature effects. These findings demonstrate that MACE-driven MD can be used as an effective high-throughput prescreening tool for defect-related studies in 2D materials, specially related to sorption. While conventional first-principles methods, such as DFT, remain necessary for accurate and quantitative validation, the use of MLIPs enables MD simulations of finite-temperature defect behavior at a fraction of the computational cost of DFT-based MD.

A Berry-curvature dipole can produce a nonlinear Hall current even when the linear Hall response vanishes, but symmetry alone does not determine its magnitude or magnetic tunability. The interplay of structural symmetry, moment orientation, and carrier occupation is examined in a honeycomb model. Curvature maps and the band-summed dipole integrand reveal how velocity and the occupation window near the Fermi level select signed contributions. Removing threefold rotation permits a nonmagnetic dipole perpendicular to the surviving mirror. Generic magnetic reorientation activates the second component and tunes both components through positive and negative values. Global reversal preserves the dipole while reversing the intrinsic linear Hall conductivity, allowing a finite bulk dipole contribution from equally populated reversed domains under uniform-field averaging.A symmetry-constrained polynomial model predicts both dipole components for 256 held-out spin configurations, achieving coefficients of determination $R^2 > 0.9995$ at the reference chemical potential. At fixed carrier density, orientation-dependent shifts of the chemical potential modify the response and yield slightly larger prediction errors for the chosen model. Across the chemical-potential sweep,the prediction accuracy decreases more strongly for $D_y$,revealing an energy dependence of the surrogate's performance. Within semiclassical transport with a constant relaxation time, the calculated dipole determines the angular dependence of the quadratic current and its rectified and second-harmonic components. These results provide a quantitative representation of magnetic-orientation-dependent Berry-curvature dipoles and show how carrier occupation influences both the response and its predictability.
